Further, if the limit exists, one says that the curve $\gamma$ lands at $\lim_{r\rightarrow1}{\gamma(r)}$. A point $a \in \partial U$ is called accessible from $U$ if some curve lands at $a$.

passages.source: \subsection*{Theorem 3.10}{(Fatou, M. Riesz, F. Riesz)}: For almost every point $e^{i\theta} \in \mathbb{D}$, the image of the radial line $r \rightarrow re^{i\theta}$ lands. However, for a fixed $u_0 \in \partial U$, the set of $\theta$ for which the image of the radial line $r \rightarrow re^{i\theta}$ lands at $u_0$ has Lebesgue measure $0$.
So far, for almost all $\theta \in (0, 2\pi]$, the function $\phi^{-1}$ gives us a good candidate for $\phi^{-1}(e^{i\theta})$. In fact, one also has the following interesting inverse statement.

\subsection*{Theorem 3.11}{(Accesses and Radial Limits)}: Let $R$ be the Riemann map, $R:\mathbb{D} \rightarrow U$ and $\gamma: [0,1) \rightarrow U$ be a curve
      which lands at a point $z_0$ in the boundary of $U$. Then the curve $R^{-1} \circ \gamma$ in $\mathbb{D}$ lands at some point $\zeta$ of $\partial\mathbb{D}$, and $R$ has the radial limit at $\zeta$ equal to $z_0$. Moreover, if $\gamma_1, \gamma_2: [0,1) \rightarrow U$ are curves landing at a common point $z_0 \in \partial U$, then $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$ are in the same access to $z_0$ if and only if $R^{-1}(\gamma_1)$ and $R^{-1}(\gamma_2)$ land at the same point in $\partial \mathbb{D}$.

To ensure continuous extension to $\partial U$ or $\partial \mathbb{D}$ one must ensure that for any sequence $\{z_j\}_j$, $z_j \rightarrow e^{i\theta}$, one has $\phi^{-1}(z_j) \rightarrow \phi^{-1}(e^{i\theta})$.

\subsection*{Definition 3.12}{(Crosscuts)}: By a crosscut for the pair $(U, \partial U)$ we mean a subset $A \subset U$ homeomorphic to $(0, 1)$ whose closure is homeomorphic to $[0,1]$ with only two endpoints in $\partial U$.

Note that $U \cong \mathbb{D}$ and for all sequences $\{x_i\}_i$, $x_i \rightarrow x \in \partial U$, we have that the accumulation points of $\{\phi(x_i)\}_i$ belong to $\partial \mathbb{D}$. This leads to a homeomorphism,
      $$\tilde{\phi}: \overline{U}/\partial U \rightarrow \overline{\mathbb{D}}/\partial \mathbb{D} \cong S^2$$

Let the crosscut $A$ be seen as a Jordan curve in $S^2$, then by the Jordan curve theorem $A$ will divide $U$ into two regions $U^+$ and $U^-$ (the signs are assigned depending on the orientation of $A$). The domains $U^+$ and $U^-$ shall be referred to as crosscut domains.

\subsection*{Definition 3.13}{(Fundamental Chains and Prime Ends)}: By a fundamental chain $\mathcal{N} = \{N_j\}_j$ in $U$, we mean a nested sequence of crosscut neighbourhoods $N_j \subset U$ such that their corresponding crosscut closures $\overline{A_j}$ are disjoint and such that their diameters tend to $0$. Two fundamental chains $\{N_j\}_j$ and $\{N_j'\}_j$ are said to be equivalent if every $N_j$ contains some $N_k'$ and vice versa. An equivalence class of fundamental chains is called a prime end for the pair $(\overline{U}, \partial U)$ (usually denoted by $\mathcal{E}$).
The following propositions collect basic properties of fundamental chains.

\subsection*{Proposition 3.14}{(Properties of Fundamental Chains I)}: For any fundamental chain $\{N_j\}_j$, the intersection of open sets $N_j$ is empty. However, the impression, $\cap \overline{N_j}$ is a non-empty compact connected subset of $\partial U$.
\subsection*{Proposition 3.15}{(Properties of Fundamental Chains II)}: Any two fundamental chains are either equivalent or eventually disjoint.
\subsection*{Proposition 3.16}{(Properties of Fundamental Chains III)}: Fundamental chains are conformal invariants.
In light of the propositions above the following is natural.

\subsection*{Definition 3.17}{(Carath\'eodory Compactification)}: Let $\mathcal{E}$ be the prime end for $(\overline{U}, \partial U)$, then $\hat{U}$, the compactification is defined to be:
        $$\hat{U}:= U\bigsqcup\left(\bigsqcup_{\mathcal{N} \in \mathcal{E}}{\mathcal{N}}\right)$$

Having seen all this, clearly, $\overline{\mathbb{D}} \cong \hat{\mathbb{D}} \cong \hat{U}$. So, to be able to extend continuously to the boundary one merely has to compare the topology of $\hat{U}$ with that of $\overline{U}$. This enabled Carath\'eodory to establish a criterion for continuous boundary extensions dependent only on the topological structure of the boundary of $U$. In particular, it is independent of the map $\phi$.
\subsection*{Theorem 3.18}{(Carath\'eodory's Theorem)}: $\phi: \mathbb{D} \rightarrow U$ a conformal isomorphism, extends continuously to the boundary $\iff$ $\partial U$ is locally connected.
Carath\'eodory's theorem can be easily extended to the case of quasiconformal maps.

\subsection*{Theorem 3.19}{(Carath\'eodory's Theorem for Quasiconformal Maps)}: Let $f:\mathbb{D}\rightarrow G$ be quasiconformal, where $G$ is a Jordan domain. Then $f$ extends continuously to the boundary.
In fact, something stronger can be said about the regularity of the boundary extension in the theorem above. For that, let us introduce two objects.
$\forall$ $z_1, z_2, z_3 \in \mathbb{S}^1$.

\subsection*{Definition 3.21}{(Quasiarcs)}: A Jordan curve $\gamma$ is called a quasiarc if $\exists$ $C>0$ such that the diameter of the smaller arc of $\gamma$ joining $z_1$ and $z_2$ is dominated by $C|z_1 - z_2|$ ($\forall$ $z_1, z_2 \in \gamma$). If the curve is closed, we shall call it a quasicircle, and the domains bounded by quasicircles shall be called quasidiscs.

The boundary extension in Theorem $3.19$ is quasisymmetric. This takes care of the first of the two questions raised before as satisfactorily as the answer given by Carath\'eodory for conformal boundary extensions did. In the interest of answering the second question and also connecting the two objects that were just introduced, let us state two theorems.

\subsection*{Theorem 3.23}{(Domain to Boundary)}: Let $G$ be a Jordan domain, $\gamma := \partial G$, and let $f: \mathbb{D} \rightarrow G$ be a conformal isomorphism, then $f$ admits a quasisymmetric extension to $\mathbb{S}^1$ $\iff$ $\gamma$ is a quasicircle.

\subsection*{Theorem 3.24}{(Boundary to Domain)}: Let $f:\mathbb{S}^1 \rightarrow \mathbb{S}^1$ be an orientation preserving quasisymmetric homeomorphism. Then $\exists \hat{f}$, $\hat{f}: \overline{\mathbb{D}} \rightarrow \overline{\mathbb{D}}$ such that $\hat{f}\big|_{\mathbb{D}}$ is quasiconformal.

For domains other than the unit disc, quasiconformal filling reduces to constructing an interpolation between the boundary maps. But saying something for a general domain is difficult, for we don't have the tools to capture all its analytic qualities. Most of these domain extensions use quite a lot of analytic properties of the domains, of them all, perhaps the most crucial is in making choices about certain covering spaces it admits. We however have annular versions of Theorem $3.23$ and Theorem $3.24$, and it shall suffice for our purposes.

\subsection*{Theorem 3.25}{(Annular Version of Theorem $3.23$)}: Let $A$ be a Jordan annulus, $\mathbb{A}_r$, the standard annulus bounded by the unit circle and the circle of radius $r$, and $f:\mathbb{A}_r \rightarrow A$ a conformal isomorphism. Let $\gamma^i$ and $\gamma^o$ denote its inner and outer boundaries. Then $f$ has a quasisymmetric extension to $\mathbb{S}^1$, $S_r^1$ $:= \{z|$ $|z| = r\}$ $\iff$ $\gamma^i$ and $\gamma^o$ are both quasicircles.

\subsection*{Theorem 3.26}{(Annular Version of Theorem $3.24$)}: For $0<r_1<r_2<1$, let $f_1:\mathbb{S}^1 \rightarrow \mathbb{S}^1$, $f_2:\mathbb{S}^1_{r_1} \rightarrow \mathbb{S}^1_{r_2}$ be two orientation preserving quasisymmetric homeomorphisms $\implies$ $\exists$ $f$, $f: \overline{\mathbb{A}}_{r_1}\rightarrow \overline{\mathbb{A}}_{r_2}$ such that its restriction on $\overline{\mathbb{A}}_{r_1}$ is quasiconformal.

Having laid out the theory necessary for surgical constructions let us briefly reiterate it by listing the essential tools one would need. In order, they are:
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item \textbf{Measurable Riemann Mapping Theorem}. It shall play the role of a scalpel by instigating any surgical procedure.
            \item \textbf{Invariant Beltrami Forms} will be our forceps, holding the incision for as many deformations as one would desire.
            \item \textbf{Theorems on Boundary and Domain Extensions} shall be the actual tools that one would need to fundamentally change the nature of a self map.
            \item \textbf{Weyl's Lemma} returns the construction to the holomorphic category.
        \end{enumerate}

Now, there are certain rules to follow. One should know when these tools can successfully be applied, and that too in the order that they have been listed above. For that, we have the following theorems which shall in some sense be our principles. The theorems illustrate instances where some of these tools can be applied, hence we shall call them surgical principles\footnote{The ones presented here are different from Shishikura's Principles. They are not needed for the constructions that follow.}.

passages.source: \subsection*{Theorem 3.27}{(Principle I)}: If $\Gamma$ is a quasiarc and $\phi: U \rightarrow V$, a homeomorphism that is $K$-qc on $U\backslash \Gamma$. Then $\phi$ is $K$-qc on $U$. (Note: As a consequence, if the boundary pieces are regular enough, one can construct global qc maps by gluing them along such boundary pieces).

\subsection*{Theorem 3.28}{(Principle II)}: Let $U \subset \mathbb{C}$ be open, $C \subset U$ compact, $\phi$ and $\Phi$ two mappings $U\rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ which are homeomorphisms. Suppose $\phi$ is qc, and so is $\Phi$ on $U\backslash C$, and that $\phi = \Phi$ on $C$. Then $\Phi$ is quasiconformal. (Note: This is referred to as Rickman's Lemma).

\subsection*{Theorem 3.29}{(Principle III)}: Let $f: \hat{\mathbb{C}} \rightarrow \hat{\mathbb{C}}$ be quasiregular. If $\exists$ $K$, such that $f^{\circ n}$ is $K$-quasiregular, $\forall n$, $n \geq 1$. Then $f$ is quasiconformally conjugate to a rational map. (Note: In literature, this is called the Straightening Theorem. It informs us of when the incision done on $f$ can lead us to a situation where Weyl's Lemma can be applied).

\BlogPost{first-surgery}{\emph{Sullivan's No Wandering Theorem}}, \BlogPost{second-surgery}{\emph{The Multiplier Map}}, and \BlogPost{third-surgery}{\emph{McMullen's Surgery}} present three different instances of quasiconformal surgery in complex dynamics.

\subsection*{Theorem 4.1 (No Wandering Theorem)}
        Rational maps of degree at least $2$ on $\hat{\mathbb{C}}$ have no wandering Fatou components.
The setup is the following:
$f: \hat{\mathbb{C}} \rightarrow \hat{\mathbb{C}}$ is a rational map,
deg$(f) \geq 2$.

A Fatou component of $f$ may be invariant, periodic, preperiodic, or wandering. Sullivan's theorem rules out the wandering case for rational maps; see \cite{branner2014quasiconformal,sullivan1985quasiconformal}. We begin with the analytic observations needed for the surgery proof.

Let $U$ be a wandering Fatou component, and let $f^{\circ n}(U) = U_n$, then $U_n \cap U_m = \varnothing$ $(\forall n \neq m)$, and since $f$ has finitely many critical points, eventually, $U_n$ will have no critical points of $f$. Conjugate $f$ by a M\"obius transform (if need be) to assume WLOG that $\infty \in f^{-1}(U)$. That is, $\infty$ belongs to a Fatou component in $f^{-1}(U)$. As all $U_n$ are disjoint, they won't intersect the component that contains $\infty$ in $f^{-1}(U)$. This forces $\bigcup_{n\geq 1}U_n$ to be bounded in $\mathbb{C}$ (after stereographic projection), as the domains $U_n$ won't cluster around $\infty$ in $\hat{\mathbb{C}}$.

Let $g$ be a non-constant limit function of the family $\{f^{\circ n}\big|_U\}_n$. Then there exists $z_0 \in U$ such that $g'(z_0) \neq 0$. Let $\overline{B_{\delta}(z_0)} \subset U$ (closed ball of radius $\delta$) be such that $g$ is injective on it. Set,
        $$\epsilon = \inf_{z\in \partial B_{\delta}(z_0)}{|g(z)-g(z_0)|}$$

Let $f^{\circ n_j}\rightarrow g$ uniformly on compact subsets of $U$. Going by first principles, $\exists J$ such that $\forall j$, $j\geq J$, $|f^{\circ n_j}(z)-g(z)| < \epsilon$ $(\forall z \in \overline{B_{\delta}(z_0)})$. Set $F_j(z):= f^{\circ n_j}(z)-g(z_0)$ and $G(z):= g(z)-g(z_0)$. Then $\forall j > J$, and $z\in \partial B_{\delta}(z_0)$,
        $$|F_j(z) -G(z)| = |f^{\circ n_j}(z)-g(z)|<\epsilon \leq |G(z)|$$

$\implies$ $G(z)$ and $F_j(z)$ have the same number of zeroes in $B_{\delta}(z_0)$ (by Rouch\'e's Theorem). So, $\forall j \geq J$, $\exists$ $z^*(j)$ such that $f^{\circ n_j}(z^*(j)) = g(z_0)$. This gives,
        $$g(z_0) \in \bigcap_{j\geq J}{U_{n_j}}$$

$\implies$ $U$ isn't a wandering domain $\implies$ $g$ is constant. Geometrically speaking, what we essentially proved is that if $g$ isn't a constant map, then Rouch\'e's Theorem and Open Mapping Theorem force all sufficiently late images of $U$ to lie in $g(U)$ and share a common point.

This forces $\operatorname{diam}(f^{\circ n}(L)) \rightarrow 0$ for every compact $L\Subset U$. If not, then $\exists L$, $L \subset U$, compact in $U$, and a subsequence $\{n_j\}_j$ such that diam$(f^{\circ n_j}(L)) \geq \delta$. Normality yields another subsequence which we shall again denote by $\{n_j\}_j$ such that $f^{\circ n_j} \rightarrow (z\rightarrow c)$ (the constant function $c$). This implies $f^{\circ n_j}(L) \subset B_{\epsilon}(c)$ $(\forall \epsilon >0)$. Contradiction.

Replace $U$ by $U_n$ for $n$ large enough so that $U_n$ has no critical points $\implies$ $f:U_n \rightarrow U_{n+1}$ will be a covering map of degree $(\leq $ deg$(f))$. Let $\gamma \subset U$ be a Jordan curve, set $\gamma_n:= f^{\circ n}(\gamma) \subset U_n$. By the above argument, we will have diam$(\gamma_n) \rightarrow 0$, hence, if $D_n$ denotes the bounded connected component of $\hat{\mathbb{C}}\backslash \gamma_n$, then diam$(D_n) \rightarrow 0$. As $\infty \in f^{-1}(U)$, by continuity of $f$ we have a $\delta >0$ such that $f(B_{\delta}(P)) \subset f^{-1}(U)$ for any pole $P$ of $f$. Now as poles are finite, for $n$ large enough, $D_n$ will contain no poles of $f$ $\implies$ $D_n$ will wander off an open ball of radius $\delta$ around each pole, since $U$ is a wandering domain.

Now set $\overline{\gamma_n}$ to be the curve $\gamma_n$ along with all its bounded components (seen as domains in $\mathbb{C}$). By the observation made above, $f\big|_{\overline{\gamma_n}}$ is holomorphic. By maximum modulus principle $f^{\circ m}$ is bounded on $\overline{\gamma_n}$, for all $m\geq n$, as $\bigcup_{m\geq n}U_m$ is bounded in $\mathbb{C}$. By Montel's Theorem, $\{f^{\circ m}\big|_{\overline{\gamma_n}}\}_m$ is a normal family $\implies$ $\overline{\gamma_n} \subset U_n$. Therefore by Jordan Curve Theorem $\gamma_n$ is null-homotopic. Lift that homotopy to $U$ to get that \textbf{$\mathbf{\{U_n\}_n}$ is a sequence of eventually simply connected domains}.

Finally, $f:U_n \rightarrow U_{n+1}$ is proper (for $\hat{\mathbb{C}}$ is compact) and a local diffeomorphism $\implies$ $f$ is a covering map. By Uniformisation Theorem we have a lift of $f$, $\tilde{f}$.

$$\begin{tikzcd}[column sep = large, row sep = large]
        U_n \arrow[r, "f"] \arrow[d, "\phi"']
        & U_{n+1} \arrow[d, "\xi"] \\
        \mathbb{D} \arrow[r,"\tilde{f}"']
        & \mathbb{D}
        \end{tikzcd}$$

This gives us that $\mathbf{f}$ \textbf{is univalent}. Henceforth replace $U$ by $U_n$ for $n$ large enough such that it is simply connected and $f$ on it is univalent.
With the two observations in bold, the stage is set for surgery modulo relevant technicalities which we shall reveal first.

\subsection*{Lemma 4.1}{(Constructing a Family of Diffeomorphisms)}: Let $B:= \{\lambda \in \mathbb{R}^N|$ $|\lambda| \leq 1\}$, $N>4d+2$, where $d = $ deg$(f)$. Given $k>1$ there exists a family of maps $\psi:B\times \overline{\mathbb{D}} \rightarrow \overline{\mathbb{D}}$, given by, $\psi(\lambda, z) \rightarrow \psi_{\lambda}(z)$ such that the following hold:
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item $\psi_{\lambda}$ is $K$-qc on $\mathbb{D}$ $(\forall \lambda \in B)$.
            \item $\psi_{\lambda}(z)$ is real analytic in $\lambda$.
            \item $\psi_0$ is identity on $\mathbb{D}$.
            \item $\psi_{\lambda}(z) = z$ ($\forall z, arg(z) \in [\pi, 2\pi], \forall \lambda \in B)$.
            \item $\psi_{\lambda_1}(z) \ncong \psi_{\lambda_2}(z)$ $(\forall \lambda_1 \neq \lambda_2$ on $\partial \mathbb{D})$.
        \end{enumerate}
\textit{Proof.}: Set,

$$w_{\delta}(x) :=
        \begin{cases}
        \delta^2\text{exp}\left(\frac{-\delta^2}{\delta^2 - x^2}\right), &\quad|x| < \delta\\
        0, &\quad|x| \geq \delta\\
        \end{cases}$$

Then, $0\leq w_{\delta}(x) \leq \frac{\delta^2}{e}$ and $|w_{\delta}'(x)| \leq \frac{8\delta}{e^2}$.
        Let $0 = x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_N<x_{N+1} = \pi$ be a partition of $[0,\pi]$ and let $\delta < \frac{1}{2}\min_{j}{(x_j-x_{j-1})}$. Define,
$$\Omega(\lambda, \theta):= \sum_{j=1}^{N}{\lambda_jw_{\delta}(\theta - x_j)}$$
$(\lambda = (\lambda_1, \lambda_2,\ldots,\lambda_n))$. With this we construct a function $\psi_{\lambda}:B\times\overline{\mathbb{D}} \rightarrow \overline{\mathbb{D}}$ as follows,

$$\psi_{\lambda}(re^{i\theta}) :=
        \begin{cases}
        re^{i(\theta+\Omega(\lambda, \theta))}, &\quad r\neq0\\
        0, &\quad r =0\\
        \end{cases}$$

Clearly, $\psi_{\lambda}$ satisfies all the conditions of the Lemma, to check quasiconformality one merely has to change one's coordinates to polar and compute $\left|\frac{\partial \bar{z}}{\partial z}(\psi_{\lambda}(z))\right|$.

\subsection*{Lemma 4.2}{(Incision)}: Let $\{\phi_t\}_{t\in[0,1]}$ be a continuous family of self-conjugacies of a rational map $f$. If $\phi_0$ is the identity, then every $\phi_t$ is the identity on the Julia set of $f$ and sends each Fatou component of $f$ to itself.

\textit{Proof.}: $\phi_t\circ f = f\circ \phi_t$ $\implies$ $\phi_t\circ f^{\circ n} = f^{\circ n}\circ \phi_t$ $\implies$ $\phi_t(\{z\in \hat{\mathbb{C}}|$ $f^{\circ n}(z) = z, \text{for some}  n\}) = \{z\in \hat{\mathbb{C}}|$ $f^{\circ n}(z)=z, \text{for some}  n\}$. Since $P_n:= \{z\in \hat{\mathbb{C}}|$ $f^{\circ n}(z)=z\}$ is discrete, $\phi_0 = \text{Id}$, and $\phi_t$ is continuous in $t$, we have, $\phi_t\big|_{P_n} = \text{Id}\big|_{P_n}$. Now $\bigcup_{n\geq1}P_n$ is dense in the Julia set, so it forces $\phi_t\big|_{J(f)} = \text{Id}$.  Let $U$ be a Fatou component, as $\phi_t$ is orientation preserving, $\phi_t\big|_{\partial U} = \text{Id}$ gives us $\phi_t\big|_{U} = U$.

\subsection*{Lemma 4.3}{(Contradiction)}: Let $U\subset \mathbb{C}$ be simply connected, $\{\phi_t\}_{t\in[0,1]}$ a family of qc-maps which extend to $\partial \mathbb{D}$ identically. Let $R:U\rightarrow \mathbb{D}$ be a Riemann map, set $\hat{\phi}_t = R\circ \phi_t\circ R^{-1}:\mathbb{D} \rightarrow \mathbb{D}$, then $\hat{\phi}_t$ extends to $\partial \mathbb{D}$ independent of $t$.

\textit{Proof.}: $\hat{\phi}_t: \mathbb{D} \rightarrow \mathbb{D}$ is quasiconformal $\implies$ $\hat{\phi}_t$ extends quasisymmetrically to $\partial \mathbb{D}$. $\phi_t$ (by Lemma $4.2$) fixes $\partial \mathbb{D}$ $\implies$ it permutes the homotopy classes of curves $\gamma:[0,1]\rightarrow U$ such that $\lim_{t\rightarrow 1}{\gamma(t)} \in \partial U$. Now $\hat{\phi}_t$ permutes points $\zeta \in \mathbb{S}^1$ such that $\lim_{r\rightarrow 1}{R(re^{i\text{arg}(\zeta)})}$ are the same, where $R$ is the Riemann map. Such points have a totally disconnected topology (by Theorem $3.11$). $\hat{\phi}_t$ is continuous in $t$, and $\hat{\phi}_t$ permutes points in the same way $\forall t$. This implies the extension of $\hat{\phi}_t$ to $\mathbb{S}^1$ is independent of $t$.
We now prove the No Wandering Theorem using the three lemmas above.

We have by Lemma $4.1$ a family of $K$-qc maps $\{\psi_{\lambda}\}_{\lambda \in B}$ with the prescribed properties. Let $\tilde{\mu}_{\lambda}:= \psi_{\lambda}^*\mu_0$, the Beltrami form induced by $\psi_{\lambda}$ on $\mathbb{D}$. Let $R:\mathbb{D} \rightarrow U$ be a Riemann map, and $\theta_1, \theta_2, \theta_3 \in [\pi, 2\pi]$ be such that,

$$
        \lim_{r \rightarrow 1}{R(re^{i\theta_j})}$$

exists $(\forall j$, $1\leq j\leq 3)$, let those limits be $a_1, a_2, a_3$, respectively. Push $\tilde{\mu}_{\lambda}$ from $\mathbb{D}$ onto $U$, i.e. let $\mu_{\lambda}:= R_*\tilde{\mu}_{\lambda}$ (aka pullback via $R^{-1}$). With these scalpels firm in our hands, let us expand the zone of possible incisions by spreading $\mu_{\lambda}$ on almost all of $\hat{\mathbb{C}}$. We do that as follows:

$\mu_{\lambda}$ has dilatation bounded by $K$, is $f$-invariant, and is real analytic in $\lambda$. By Mapping Theorem we have $\phi_{\lambda}:\hat{\mathbb{C}} \rightarrow \hat{\mathbb{C}}$ such that $\phi_{\lambda}^*\mu_0 = \mu_{\lambda}$. Let $g_{\lambda} = \phi_{\lambda}\circ f\circ \phi_{\lambda}^{-1}$ $\implies$ By Weyl's Lemma $g_{\lambda}$ is holomorphic, as $g_{\lambda}^*\mu_0= (\phi^{-1}_{\lambda})^* \circ (f)^*\circ (\phi_{\lambda})^*\mu_0 = (\phi^{-1}_{\lambda})^*\circ (f^*\mu_{\lambda}) = (\phi^{-1}_{\lambda})^*\mu_{\lambda} = \mu_0$. We can further arrange for $\phi_{\lambda}$ such that it fixes $a_1, a_2, a_3$, and depends analytically on $\lambda$. $g_{\lambda}$ is a rational map of the same degree $d$ as that of $f$ (for $\phi_{\lambda}$ are mere homeomorphisms) $\implies$ the $2d+1$ coefficients of $g_{\lambda}$ depend analytically on $\lambda$ by construction. Define,
$$\pi: B \rightarrow \text{Rat}_d,   \pi(\lambda) := g_{\lambda}$$

Real dimension of $\text{Rat}_d$ is $2(2d+1) = 4d+2$ (since $\text{dim}(B)>4d+2$). This gives rise to a path $\lambda:[0,1] \rightarrow B$, such that $g_{\lambda(t)} = g$, $\forall t, t\in [0,1]$ (because $\exists$ $g_{\lambda} \in \text{Rat}_d$ such that it is a regular value of $\pi$, for $\psi_{\lambda}$ is injective on $\lambda$). Set $\Phi_t = \phi^{-1}_{\lambda(0)}\circ \phi_{\lambda(t)}$. We have the following:
Therefore, with the help of the scalpels $\psi_{\lambda}$ the incision we made leaves us with the following parametrized deformations.

Consider $\hat{\Phi}_t: (\mathbb{D}, \tilde{\mu}_{\lambda(t)}) \rightarrow (\mathbb{D}, \tilde{\mu}_{\lambda(0)})$, where $\hat{\Phi}_t := R\circ \Phi_t\circ R^{-1}$. Now by Lemma $4.3$ $\hat{\Phi}_t$ extends to $\hat{\Phi}$ on $\partial \mathbb{D}$ (independent of $t$). This gives us,
$$\hat{\psi}_t := \psi_{\lambda(0)}\circ \hat{\Phi}_t: (\mathbb{D}, \tilde{\mu}_{\lambda(t)}) \rightarrow (\mathbb{D}, \mu_0)$$
as shown in the diagram below,

$$\begin{tikzcd}[column sep = large, row sep = large]

        \\

        \arrow[r, "\text{Id}"']

where $\hat{\psi}_t$ extends to $\partial \mathbb{D}$ (given by $\psi_{\lambda(0)}\circ \hat{\Phi}$). Note that $\psi_{\lambda(t)}$ and $\hat{\psi}_t$ pull back the same Beltrami form ($\tilde{\mu}_{\lambda(t)}$), and they both fix $a_1, a_2, a_3$ $\implies$ by Weyl's Lemma $\psi_{\lambda(t)} = \hat{\psi}_t$. This exposes the following,
$$\psi_{\lambda(t)}\Big|_{\partial \mathbb{D}} = (\psi_{\lambda(0)} \circ \hat{\Phi}_t)\Big|_{\partial \mathbb{D}} = \psi_{\lambda(0)}\circ \hat{\Phi}$$
$\forall t$, $t\in[0,1]$ $\implies$ $\psi_{\lambda(t)}\big|_{\partial\mathbb{D}}$ is independent of $t$, contradicting Lemma $4.1$ $(5)$.
$\qed$
The argument below is developed in greater detail in \cite{branner2014quasiconformal}, \cite{MR812271}, and \cite{MR762431}. We shall prove the following theorem.

\subsection*{Theorem 5.1 (Multiplier Map for a Unicritical Polynomial)}
    Let $\Omega$ be a hyperbolic component of $\mathcal{M}_d$ for $d\geq2$, and let $c^*$ be its centre. Then the multiplier map
    \[
    \Lambda_d:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb{D}
    \]
    is a proper holomorphic map of degree $d-1$, with $\Lambda_d^{-1}(0)=\{c^*\}$ and local degree $d-1$ at $c^*$. Equivalently,
    \[
    \Lambda_d:\Omega\backslash\{c^*\}\longrightarrow\mathbb{D}^*
    \]
    is an unbranched $(d-1)$-sheeted covering.

Fix a point $c_0 \in \Omega^*$ with $\Lambda_d(c_0) = \lambda_0 \neq 0$. Choose an arbitrary simply connected neighbourhood $U_0$ of $\lambda_0$, compactly contained in $\mathbb{D}^*$. Here the unicritical family has degree $d$ and is parametrized by polynomials of the form $Q_c(z) = z^d +c$. For any $\lambda \in U_0$ we shall construct a monic centred polynomial $Q_{c(\lambda)}(z) = z^d + c(\lambda)$, which is quasiconformally conjugate to $Q_{c_0}$ and satisfies, $c(\lambda_0) = c_0$, $\Lambda_d(c(\lambda)) = \lambda,$ and $\lambda \rightarrow c(\lambda)$ is holomorphic. It would follow that $c(\lambda) \in \Omega^*$, and that we would have constructed a holomorphic local inverse of $\Lambda_d$ in the neighbourhood $U_0$ of $\lambda_0$. Therefore $\Lambda_d: \Omega^* \rightarrow \mathbb{D}^*$ will turn out to be a holomorphic covering map.

The Koenigs coordinate of the polynomial $Q_{c_0} = f_{\lambda_0}$ can be surgically transformed to a linear map with a different multiplier as in \BlogPost{the-mapping-theorem-and-invariant-complex-structures}{\emph{The Mapping Theorem and Invariant Complex Structures}}. One can then spread the altered Beltrami form to the whole basin of attraction of a given cycle. More precisely, choose a branch of the logarithm on $U_0$, set $v=\log\lambda$ and $v_0=\log\lambda_0$, and let $L_v$ be the real-linear map such that $L_v\circ (\zeta\rightarrow \zeta+v_0)\circ L_v^{-1}=\zeta\rightarrow\zeta+v$. Let $\{\alpha_0, \alpha_1,\ldots, \alpha_{p-1}\}$ be the attracting cycle, let $\mathcal{A}(\alpha) = \mathcal{A}_f(\alpha)$ denote the basin of attraction of the cycle. Then note that the Koenigs map extends to the whole basin of attraction $\mathcal{A}_{f^p}(\alpha_0)$ of $\alpha_0$ as a fixed point of $f^p_{\lambda_0}$. Let $\psi_0$ be the extended linearizing map of $f^p_{\lambda_0}$, then we would have $\psi_0(\mathcal{A}_{f^p}(\alpha_0)) = \mathbb{C}$.

So, pull back $\hat{\mu}_{\lambda}$ via the map $f_{\lambda_0}$ and spread it across $\mathcal{A}(\alpha)$ and set $\hat{\mu}_{\lambda} = 0$ in the complement of $\mathcal{A}(\alpha)$. This gives us an altered Beltrami form on the whole sphere, and mapping theorem now gives us an integrating map $\hat{\phi}_{\lambda}$ such that the following commutes.

$$\begin{tikzcd}[column sep = large, row sep = large]
        (\hat{\mathbb{C}}, \hat{\mu}_{\lambda})

Further, the integrating map $\hat{\phi}_{\lambda}$ can be arranged\footnote{The point behind arranging for $\hat{\phi}_{\lambda}$ satisfying that limit is that having conjugated $f_{\lambda_0}$ such that $\mathcal{A}(\alpha)$ does not contain $\infty$, implies it lies around $\infty$, further $\hat{\mu}_{\lambda} = 0$, so one can arrange for $\hat{\phi}_{\lambda} \sim \text{Id}$ around $\infty$} so that $\frac{\hat{\phi}_{\lambda}}{z} \rightarrow 1$ as $z \rightarrow \infty$, so that if $\hat{\phi}_{\lambda}$ conjugates $f_{\lambda_0}$ and $f_{\lambda}$, then $f_{\lambda}$ is already a monic centred polynomial of degree $d$ with one critical point at $0$ and with a $p$-cycle of multiplier $\lambda$ (as the number of preimages of a given point shall remain fixed). These imply that $f_{\lambda}(z) = z^d + c(\lambda)$, and moreover as $\hat{\phi}_{\lambda}(f_{\lambda_0}(0)) = f_{\lambda}(\hat{\phi}_{\lambda}(0))$, we have $c(\lambda) = \hat{\phi}_{\lambda}(c_0)$, the critical value of $f_{\lambda}$. It is clear that if $\alpha_0$ is one of the points in the $p$-cycle for $Q_{c_0}$, then $\Lambda_d(c(\lambda)) = (Q^{\circ p}_{c(\lambda)})'(\hat{\phi}_{\lambda}(\alpha_0)) = \lambda$, as we wanted to show.

footnotes.source: The point behind arranging for $\hat{\phi}_{\lambda}$ satisfying that limit is that having conjugated $f_{\lambda_0}$ such that $\mathcal{A}(\alpha)$ does not contain $\infty$, implies it lies around $\infty$, further $\hat{\mu}_{\lambda} = 0$, so one can arrange for $\hat{\phi}_{\lambda} \sim \text{Id}$ around $\infty$

passages.source: The next step in the proof is to establish holomorphic dependence on parameters. Note that the Beltrami coefficient $\mu_{\lambda}$ varies holomorphically with respect to $v=\log\lambda$, hence also with respect to $\lambda$. In fact,

\[
    \mu_{\lambda}(z) = \frac{z(v-v_0)}{\bar{z}(v+\overline{v_0})}.
    \]
Therefore, for $z \in \mathcal{A}_{Q^p_{c_0}}(\alpha_0)$,
$$\lambda \rightarrow \hat{\mu}_{\lambda}$$

is holomorphic. If $p>1$, this holomorphic dependence is spread to all of $z\in \mathcal{A}(\alpha)$ by successive pullbacks with $Q_{c_0}$, independent of $\lambda$, and since $\hat{\mu}_{\lambda} = 0$ outside $\mathcal{A}(\alpha)$ it is trivially holomorphically dependent on $\lambda$. Set for all $\lambda \in U_0$,

\[
    k(\lambda) = \left|\frac{v-v_0}{v+\overline{v_0}}\right|.
    \]

Then $\lambda \rightarrow k(\lambda)$ is a continuous real valued function on $\overline{U_0}$ that takes values in $[0,1)$. Moreover, we have
    $$||\hat{\mu}_{\lambda}||_{\infty} = ||\mu_{\lambda}||_{\infty} = k(\lambda)$$

Set,
    $$k = \sup_{\lambda \in U_0}{k(\lambda)}.$$

Since $\overline{U_0}$ is compact, the supremum is realized as the maximal value of $k(\lambda)$ for $\lambda \in \overline{U_0}$. Hence $k<1$ and $||\hat{\mu}_{\lambda}||_{\infty} \leq k$ for all $\lambda \in U_0$. Therefore $\lambda \rightarrow \hat{\phi}_{\lambda}$ is holomorphic in $\lambda$ for all $z\in \mathbb{C}$. As $\hat{\phi}_{\lambda}$ is a conjugacy between $Q_{c_0}$ and $f_{\lambda}$, it maps the critical value $c_0$ of $Q_{c_0}$, to the critical value $\hat{\phi}_{\lambda}(c_0)$ of $f_{\lambda}$. Said differently,
$$f_{\lambda} = Q_{c(\lambda)}$$
where $c(\lambda) = \hat{\phi}_{\lambda}(c_0)$. Thus, $c(\lambda)$ depends holomorphically on $\lambda$.

Since the proper covering $\Lambda_d:\Omega^*\rightarrow\mathbb{D}^*$ has finite fibres and $\Omega^*$ is connected, it is a connected finite-sheeted covering. Thus $\Omega^*$ is a punctured disk; filling its puncture gives the unique centre $c^*$ of $\Omega$. Now it remains to prove that the degree of the multiplier map $\Lambda_d: \Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{D}$ is $d-1$. If $\Omega$ has period $p$, then $Q^{\circ p}_{c^*}(0)=0$. The following lemma of Gleason completes the proof.
\subsection*{Lemma 5.2}: Consider the polynomials $G_n(c) = Q^n_c(0)$ for $n\geq 1$. All roots of $G_n$ are simple.
\textit{Proof.}: We have,

It follows that $G_n$ is monic with integer coefficients. The roots of $G_n$ are therefore algebraic integers over $\mathbb{Z}$. Assume that there exists an $n>1$ and a root $\tilde{c}$ of $G_n$ which is not simple. Then $\tilde{c}$ must be a root of both $G_n$ and its derivative. That is,
    $$G_n'(c) = d(G_{n-1}(c))^{d-1}G_{n-1}'(c)+1$$

It follows that,
    $$(G_{n-1}(\tilde{c}))^{d-1}G_{n-1}'(\tilde{c}) = \frac{-1}{d}$$

Since the set of algebraic integers $\mathbb{A}$ forms a ring, we have from the above equation that $\frac{-1}{d}$ is an algebraic integer. But since $\mathbb{Q}\cap\mathbb{A} = \mathbb{Z}$, $G_n$ has no multiple roots.

Note that for any $c\in \Omega$ the points in the attracting $p$-cycle are solutions of
    \[
    F(c,z) = Q_c^{\circ p}(z) - z = 0.
    \]

The map $F$ satisfies the hypothesis of the Implicit Function Theorem at the point $(c^*,0)$, since
    \[
    F_z(c^*,0)=(Q_{c^*}^{\circ p})'(0)-1=-1,
    \qquad F_c(c^*,0)=G_p'(c^*)\neq0
    \]
    by Gleason's lemma. So, in a neighbourhood of $c^*$ the points in the attracting $p$-cycle can therefore be expressed as functions of $c$. Let $\alpha_0(c)$ denote the periodic point in the Fatou component containing the critical point $0$, so $\alpha_0(c^*)=0$, and
    \[
    \alpha_0'(c^*)=-\frac{F_c(c^*,0)}{F_z(c^*,0)}=G_p'(c^*)\neq0,
    \]
    so $\alpha_0(c)$ has a simple zero at $c=c^*$. Set $\alpha_j(c)=Q_c^{\circ j}(\alpha_0(c))$ for $j=1,\ldots,p-1$. The multiplier map can be written as
    \[
    \Lambda_d(c)=(Q_c^{\circ p})'(\alpha_0(c))
    =\prod_{j=0}^{p-1}Q_c'(\alpha_j(c))
    =d^p\prod_{j=0}^{p-1}\alpha_j(c)^{d-1}.
    \]

Since $\alpha_0$ has a simple zero at $c^*$ and $\alpha_j(c^*)\neq0$ for $1\leq j<p$,
    \[
    \operatorname{ord}_{c^*}\Lambda_d
    =(d-1)\sum_{j=0}^{p-1}\operatorname{ord}_{c^*}\alpha_j
    =d-1.
    \]
    Thus the local degree of $\Lambda_d$ at $c^*$ is $d-1$. Since $\Lambda_d:\Omega^*\rightarrow\mathbb{D}^*$ is a covering, it has $d-1$ sheets. With this we conclude the proof of Theorem $5.1$.

posts.title: McMullen's Surgery I: Ideal Boundaries and the Gluing Lemma

passages.source: Let $f$ be a rational map of degree at least $2$ on $\hat{\mathbb{C}}$, and $\text{Aut}(f)$ the group of M\"obius transformations commuting with $f$. Given any such transformation $M$, for each $n$, $M$ permutes the finitely many periodic points of order $n$. Choose $n$ so that this set has at least three distinct points. The induced action of $\text{Aut}(f)$ on this finite set is faithful, since a M\"obius transformation fixing three points is the identity. Therefore, $\text{Aut}(f)$ is a finite group. We shall now attempt to loosen the regularity and see if the finiteness can be retained. To begin with, let $\text{Mod}(f)$ denote the group of isotopy classes of quasiconformal maps commuting with $f$. It can be shown that regardless of the group being infinite and complicated, all its finite subgroups can be realized as subgroups of $\text{Aut}(g)$ for some deformation $g$ of $f$. So, we pull our necks a bit more to the surface and ask what about the group $\text{Mod}(J, f)$, the group of quasiconformal maps commuting with $f$ only on its Julia set? Yet again, it can be shown that if the Julia set is connected and carries no invariant line field, then $\text{Mod}(J, f)$ is a finite group. The proof of the former claim uses Nielsen realization for Riemann surfaces and is done in \cite{mcmullen1988automorphisms}, \cite{mcmullen1998quasiconformal} and \cite{imayoshi2012introduction}; the latter claim will be our focus here. Let us define certain objects before proceeding further.

\subsection*{Definition 6.1}{(Invariant Line Field on the Julia Set)}: A line field on the Julia set $J(f)$ of $f$ is a measurable Beltrami differential $\mu(z)$, supported on a positive area subset of $J(f)$, with $|\mu(z)|=1$ almost everywhere on its support. It is said to be invariant if $f^*\mu = \mu$.

We say that two maps $\phi$, $\psi$ determine the same stable conjugacy if they are isotopic through maps satisfying the three aforementioned conditions. The group of self stable conjugacies $(F, f)$ is denoted by $\text{Mod}(F, f)$.

We shall study the finiteness of the object $\text{Mod}(K, f)$, the group of quasiconformal maps commuting with $f$ on $K$ (a forward invariant component of $J(f)$). Our main goal will be proving the following.

Now the finiteness above is only for stable conjugacies on certain components of the Julia set. In particular, one can easily deduce from the theorem above that if the Julia set is connected and admits no invariant line field then $\text{Mod}(J(f), f)$ is a finite group. It has been conjectured that the hypothesis demanding the non-existence of invariant line fields on $J(f)$ can be dropped.
\subsection*{Conjecture 6.4}: For any nonaffine rational map $g$ with connected Julia set $J$, $\text{Mod}(J, g)$ is a finite group.
At the end, we shall briefly touch upon this conjecture for the case of exposed critical points. Let us now begin the proof of Theorem $6.3$

\subsection*{Proposition 6.5}{(Rickman's Lemma)}: Let $\phi:\hat{\mathbb{C}}\rightarrow\hat{\mathbb{C}}$ be a homeomorphism and $R\subset\hat{\mathbb{C}}$ an open region. If $\phi\big|_R$ is $K$-qc and $\phi\big|_{\hat{\mathbb{C}}\backslash R} = \text{Id}\big|_{\hat{\mathbb{C}}\backslash R}$, then $\phi$ is quasiconformal \cite{mcmullen1988automorphisms}.

\textit{Proof.}: Clearly $\phi(R)=R$. Conjugate $\phi$ by $\psi_1,\psi_2\in\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ so that $\widetilde\phi=\psi_1\circ\phi\circ\psi_2^{-1}$ has two fixed points $z,w\in R$, and set $X=\hat{\mathbb C}\setminus\{z,w\}\cong\mathbb C$. The restrictions of $\widetilde\phi$ to the image of $R$ and to its complement in $X$ are quasiconformal and agree continuously because $\widetilde\phi$ is a homeomorphism. Rickman's quasiconformal pasting lemma therefore makes $\widetilde\phi$, and hence $\phi$, quasiconformal on the sphere. This is an application of the cited pasting lemma, rather than an independent proof of that lemma.

This surgery, unlike the preceding two, cuts and pastes along ideal boundaries rather than topological boundaries \cite{mcmullen1988automorphisms,branner2014quasiconformal}. So, we begin by formulating an appropriate analogue of Rickman's lemma to help us formulate a mechanism with which we can glue certain deformed objects.

\subsection*{Definition 6.6}{(Ideal Boundary of a Disc)}: By a disk $U \subset \hat{\mathbb{C}}$ we mean a simply connected domain whose complement contains at least two points. For a disk $U$, the ideal boundary $I(U)$ is the set of all prime ends of $U$.

\subsection*{Prime-end chain lemma}
    Let $\mathcal N=\langle N_j\rangle_j$ and $\mathcal M=\langle M_j\rangle_j$ be fundamental chains. Then $\mathcal N\sim\mathcal M$, or the two chains are eventually disjoint: there are $j_0,k_0$ such that $N_j\cap M_k=\varnothing$ whenever $j\geq j_0$ and $k\geq k_0$. This is the precise meaning of the notebook shorthand ``$\mathcal N\wedge\mathcal M$ eventually.''

Given a proper holomorphic map $f:U\rightarrow V$ between discs $U$ and $V$, one obtains an induced map between their respective ideal boundaries. Indeed, consider the Riemann maps $R_U:U\rightarrow \mathbb{D}$ and $R_V:V\rightarrow \mathbb{D}$, and consider the composition $\hat{f} = R_V\circ f \circ R_U^{-1}: \mathbb{D}\rightarrow\mathbb{D}$, a proper holomorphic self map. Using reflection across $\mathbb{S}^1$, namely $z\mapsto 1/\bar z$, and the Schwarz Reflection Principle, one can extend the map to a real analytic map on $\mathbb{S}^1$. Since Riemann maps give homeomorphisms between $\mathbb{S}^1$ and the corresponding ideal boundaries, we have a map $\hat{f}:I(U)\rightarrow I(V)$. It doesn't make sense to call $\hat{f}$ real analytic intrinsically, but whenever we do so we invariably see it in these circle coordinates. Now with this in mind let us formulate an analogue of Rickman's lemma.

\textit{Proof.}: $(1)$ $\phi$ is continuous on $\overline{U}$ implies $\phi$ is uniformly continuous as $\overline{U}$ is compact. Let $\{C_n\}_n$ be a sequence of crosscuts. As $\phi$ is a homeomorphism and $\text{diam}(C_n) \rightarrow 0$, uniform continuity ensures that if $\{C_n\}_n$ defines a prime end, then so does $\{\phi(C_n)\}_n$. Let $U_1 \supset U_2 \supset \cdots \supset U_n \supset \cdots$ be the prime end corresponding to $\{C_n\}$. Then an easy consequence of Jordan Curve Theorem would tell us that $C_l \subset U_k$ for all $l>k$.\\
    Set $Q_k$ to be the quadrilateral bounded by $C_k\cup C_{k+1}$ in $U$ for large $k$. Fix $n$. Suppose there exists an increasing sequence $\{k_i\}_i$ such that $Q_{k_i}$ and $\phi(Q_{k_i})$ belong to different components of $U\backslash C_n$. After passing to a subsequence, choose $x_{k_i}\in Q_{k_i}$ with $x_{k_i}\rightarrow x\in\mathcal E\subset\partial U$, where $\mathcal E$ is the impression of the prime end.\\
    As $\phi$ is uniformly continuous, $\phi(x_{k_i})\rightarrow\phi(x)=x$ ($\phi$ is identity on $\partial U$), but this forces $\phi(x_{k_i})$ and $x_{k_i}$ to eventually land in the same component of $U\backslash C_n$, a contradiction. Thus, for every fixed $n$, $\phi(U_k)\subset U_n$ for all sufficiently large $k$. Applying the same argument to $\{\phi(U_k)\}_k$ and $\phi^{-1}$ shows that the two chains define the same prime end.

(2) Observe that if $\phi$ is identity on the ideal boundary of $U$, then
    $\sup_{z\in U}d_U(\phi(z),z)<\infty$, where $d_U$ is the Poincar\'e distance on the hyperbolic surface $U\cong\mathbb D$; this is the standard bounded-displacement property of a quasiconformal self-map of the disk with identity boundary values \cite{mcmullen1988automorphisms}. Suppose this supremum is less than $K$. Given any $\{x_k\}_k$ such that $x_k\rightarrow x\in\partial U$, we have $\phi(x_k)\in B_K(x_k)$. Since $\overline U$ is compact in $\hat{\mathbb C}$ and $U$ is hyperbolic, the fixed-radius Poincar\'e balls $B_K(x_k)$ converge to $x$ in the spherical topology. In particular, $\phi(x_k)\rightarrow x$, so $\phi$ extends continuously to $\partial U$ and $\phi\big|_{\partial U}=\operatorname{Id}$. A direct application of Rickman's lemma now completes the proof.

\subsection*{Proposition 6.8}
    Let $\phi$, $\psi: \overline{U} \rightarrow \overline{V}$ be homeomorphisms where $U$ and $V$ are discs, $K$-qc on $U$ and equal on $\partial U$. Then there exists an isotopy connecting $\phi$ to $\psi$ through $K^3$-qc maps all agreeing on $\partial U$.

\textit{Proof.}: Let $\alpha = \psi^{-1}\circ \phi: U \rightarrow U$. Then $\alpha$ is $K^2$-qc and is identity on $I(U)$ by the previous proposition. We construct $\alpha_t$ connecting $\alpha$ to the identity map through homeomorphisms enjoying the two properties that $\alpha$ does. Uniformize $U$ and bring the identity in radially from the boundary of the unit disk, as in \cite{mcmullen1988automorphisms}; this gives the required isotopy through $K^2$-qc maps. Push it to $U$ and note that the desired isotopy is given by $\phi_t = \psi\circ \alpha_t$. Its maps are $K^3$-qc and agree on $\partial U$.
\subsection*{Corollary 6.9} If $K$ is connected and periodic points of $f$ are dense in $K$, then any $[\phi]$ in $\text{Mod}(K, f)$ is uniquely determined by its values on $K$.

\textit{Proof.}: Let's now construct a stable conjugacy taking $\phi$ to $\text{Id}$, given that $\phi = \text{Id}$ on $K$. Here, $K$ is compact connected. Let $\hat{\mathbb{C}}\backslash K = \sqcup_{\alpha}U_{\alpha}$, then $U_{\alpha}$'s are simply connected. Indeed, let $\gamma$ be a loop in $U_{\alpha}$, then as $\gamma \cap K = \varnothing$, one can construct a polygonal region $\tilde{\gamma}$ such that $K$ and $\gamma$ belong to different components of $\hat{\mathbb{C}}\backslash \tilde{\gamma}$. Now the claim is a simple consequence of the Jordan Curve Theorem: if $\gamma \subset \text{Int}(\tilde{\gamma})$, then $\text{Int}(\tilde{\gamma})\subseteq U_{\alpha}$. By the previous propositions, on each disk in the complement of $K$ there is an isotopy connecting $\phi$ to the identity through quasiconformal maps which are identity on $K$. The dilatation of the intervening maps is bounded by $K(\phi)^3$ (independent of the disk). By Proposition $6.5$ the time $t$ maps in each disk piece together to form a quasiconformal map of the whole Riemann sphere. Thus, $[\phi] = [\text{Id}]$ in $\text{Mod}(K,f)$.

\subsection*{Definition 6.10}{(Ideal Boundary of $K$)}: We define $I(K)$, the ideal boundary of a given infinite continuum $K$, to be the union of the ideal boundaries of the disks in the complement of $K$. Thus
    \[
    I(K):=\bigcup_{\substack{V\subseteq\hat{\mathbb C}\setminus K\\
                    V\text{ a component}}}I(V).
    \]
    (Note: In what's to follow $K$ shall be a forward invariant component of $J(f)$ unless otherwise stated).

If $f$ is quasirational (i.e. quasiconformally conjugate to a rational function on $\hat{\mathbb{C}}$), then $f$ induces a map $\hat{f}: I(K) \rightarrow I(K)$ which is quasisymmetrically conjugate to a real analytic map. Indeed, firstly assume $f$ to be rational. Since $\text{deg}(f) < \infty$, $f^{-1}(K)$ consists of $K$ and finitely many other components. Let $U$ be a component of $\hat{\mathbb{C}}\backslash K$, and let $U'$ be the component of $U\backslash f^{-1}(K)$ whose closure contains $\partial U$. Then $f$ carries $U'$ properly to a component $V$ of $\hat{\mathbb{C}}\backslash K$. In Riemann-map coordinates for $U$ and $V$, the map $f$ carries a neighbourhood of $\mathbb{S}^1$ to a neighbourhood of $\mathbb{S}^1$. By the Schwarz Reflection Principle it extends across the circle and induces a real analytic map $\hat{f}:I(U)\rightarrow I(V)$. If $f$ were now only quasirational, then the induced map on the ideal boundary of $K$ would be quasisymmetrically conjugate to a real analytic map.

\subsection*{Definition 6.11}{(Compatibility of Maps on the Ideal Boundary)}: Let $K$ be a non-degenerate invariant continuum such that $f^{-1}(K)$ consists of $K$ and finitely many other disjoint components. Let $U$ and $V$ be components of $\hat{\mathbb{C}}\backslash K$ so that $\hat{f}:I(U) \rightarrow I(V)$ as described above is the induced map. Let $B$ denote a Blaschke product mapping $\overline{\mathbb{D}}$ onto itself \cite{garcia2018finite}. We say $f$ and $B$ are compatible on the ideal boundary of $U$ via quasiconformal maps $\phi_U:U\rightarrow \mathbb{D}$ and $\phi_V:V\rightarrow \mathbb{D}$, if the induced maps $\hat{\phi}_U: I(U) \rightarrow \mathbb{S}^1$ and $\hat{\phi}_V: I(V) \rightarrow \mathbb{S}^1$ define a quasisymmetric equivalence between $\hat{f}:I(U) \rightarrow I(V)$ and the restriction of $B$ to the unit circle, as shown in the following commutative diagram:

$$\begin{tikzcd}[column sep = large, row sep = large]
        I(U)
        \arrow[d, "\hat{\phi}_U"']
        \arrow[r, "\hat{f}"]
        &
        I(V)
        \arrow[d, "\hat{\phi}_V"]
        \\
        \mathbb{S}^1
        \arrow[r, "B"']
        &
        \mathbb{S}^1
        \\
        \end{tikzcd}$$

        I(U)
        \arrow[d, "\hat{\phi}_U"']

        I(V)
        \arrow[d, "\hat{\phi}_V"]

We are now ready to state and prove the Gluing Lemma.
Assume $f$ and $B$ are compatible on $I(U)$ via maps $\phi_U$ and $\phi_V$. Then the map

$$g(z):= \begin{cases}
        f(z), &\quad\text{if}  z \notin U\\
        \phi_V^{-1}\circ B\circ \phi_U(z) &\quad\text{if}   z\in U\\
        \end{cases}$$

\textit{Proof.}: Consider locally a branch of $f^{-1}\circ g$ that agrees with the identity outside $U$, away from the finitely many branch values. In the notation of the source this is
    \[
    f^{-1}\circ g=
    \begin{cases}
    \operatorname{Id},&z\notin U,\\
    \psi\quad\text{(quasiconformal)},&z\in U.
    \end{cases}
    \]
    It also induces the identity map on the ideal boundary since $\hat{f} = \hat{\phi}_V^{-1}\circ B\circ\hat{\phi}_U = \hat{g}:I(U)\rightarrow I(V)$. Proposition $6.7$ gives the continuous identity extension across the physical boundary, and Proposition $6.5$ supplies the quasiconformal pasting. Composing with $f$ shows that $g$ is quasiregular away from the branch points; the isolated branch points are removable for quasiregular maps. Hence $g$ is quasiregular. Its dilatation is bounded by the maximum of $K(f)$ and $K(\phi_U)K(\phi_V)$.\\

The notebook also proposes a Sobolev cutoff proof of this pasting step. Let
    $u=\operatorname{Re}(\psi-\operatorname{Id})$ (and similarly take the imaginary part), so that one would need $u\in H^1$ on the indicated ball.

Its proposed inference is that $\eta_nu\to u$ and that $\eta_nu=0$ on a neighbourhood of $K$ for sufficiently large $n$, hence $u\in H^1$. Convergence without an $H^1$ estimate does not imply that conclusion, so this notebook route has a gap; the rigorous input in the preceding paragraph is Rickman's pasting lemma. The final source sketch of the same missing estimate assumes a sequence $x_k\to x$ with
    \[
    d_U\bigl(\psi(x_k),x_k\bigr)\longrightarrow\infty
    \]
    and compares the chains $\langle N_k\rangle_k$ and $\langle\psi(N_k)\rangle_k$.

The identity ideal-boundary values force these chains to be equivalent, as in the MS13 diagram above; making this into the required uniform hyperbolic-distance estimate needs the standard bounded-displacement theorem used in Proposition $6.7$.

\subsection*{Corollary 6.13} In the setup above, suppose $U_0 = U_p$, and $U_1, U_2,\ldots, U_{p-1}$ are components of $\hat{\mathbb{C}}\backslash K$ such that $\hat{f}^{\circ j}(I(U_0)) = I(U_j)$ for $0\leq j\leq p-1$. Set $\phi_p=\phi_0$. For $j = 0, 1, \ldots, p-1$, let $B_j$ be Blaschke products compatible with $f\big|_{U_j}$ on the ideal boundary via the maps $\phi_j$ and $\phi_{j+1}$. Then the map
    $$g(z):= \begin{cases}
        f(z), &\quad\text{if}  z \notin \bigcup_{j=0}^{p-1}{U_j}\\
        \phi_{j+1}^{-1}\circ B_j\circ \phi_j(z) &\quad\text{if}   z\in U_j\\
        \end{cases}$$
is quasirational.

\textit{Proof.}: Note that $g^{\circ p}$ is quasiconformally conjugate to a Blaschke product of degree $d = \prod_{j=0}^{p-1}{\text{deg}(B_j)}$ on any of the $U_j$'s. Since the cycle contains only finitely many $U_j$, this bound is uniform on their union, while the original bound for $f$ applies off the cycle. Therefore, $K(g^{\circ n})$ is uniformly bounded forcing $g$ to be quasirational by Straightening Theorem.

posts.title: McMullen's Surgery II: Rigid Models and a Julia Component

passages.source: In \BlogPost{third-surgery}{Part I}, the Gluing Lemma gave us the mechanism for cutting and pasting along ideal boundaries. One of the means of carrying out this successive surgery would be by pasting certain rigid models, defined as follows:

\subsection*{Definition 6.14}{(Rigid Models)}: We give here three rigid models for proper self maps of the unit disk as:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item The elliptic model $z\rightarrow e^{2\pi i\theta}z$, for $\theta \in \mathbb{R}\backslash \mathbb{Q}$,
        \item The hyperbolic model $z\rightarrow z^d$ for some $d>1$,
        \item The parabolic model $z \rightarrow P_d(z)$ for $d>1$, where
        $$P_d(z):= \frac{z^d + a}{1+az^d}   \text{for}   a = \frac{d-1}{d+1}$$
    \end{enumerate}

Let $M_a(z)=(z+a)/(1+az)$. The composition in the notes is correctly read as $P_d=M_a\circ(z\mapsto z^d)$. If $|z|=1$ and $z=x+iy$, then
    \[
    \begin{aligned}
    |z+a|^2&=|1+az|^2,\\
    (x+a)^2+y^2&=(1+ax)^2+a^2y^2,\\
    (x^2+y^2)(1-a^2)+a^2&=1.
    \end{aligned}
    \]
    The last equality follows from $x^2+y^2=1$, and proves $|P_d(z)|=1$ on $\mathbb S^1$.

Thus $P_d(\mathbb{S}^1)=\mathbb{S}^1$, and $P_d$ is orientation-preserving. Hence $P_d(\mathbb{D})=\mathbb{D}$ and $P_d(\widehat{\mathbb{C}}\setminus\overline{\mathbb{D}})=\widehat{\mathbb{C}}\setminus\overline{\mathbb{D}}$. By Montel's theorem, $P_d$ is normal on $\mathbb{D}$ and $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}\setminus\overline{\mathbb{D}}$. Since $\mathbb{S}^1$ is their common boundary, $J(P_d)=\mathbb{S}^1$.

Let $B(z) = e^{2\pi i\theta}z$, and let $\phi$ be an orientation preserving circle homeomorphism such that $\phi\circ B = B\circ\phi$. A lift initially satisfies $F(z+\theta)=F(z)+\theta+k$ for some integer $k$, while $F(z+1)=F(z)+1$. Since $F(z)-z$ is bounded and iterating the first identity would produce the term $nk$, we must have $k=0$. Thus $F(z+\theta) = F(z) + \theta$, and $F(z)-z$ is $1$-periodic. This implies $F(m\theta + n) = F(0) + m\theta+n$; now as $m\theta + n$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$, we get that $F(z) = z+\alpha$ $\implies$ $\phi$ is a rotation.\\

Indeed,
    \[
    P_d'(z)=\frac{d(1-a^2)z^{d-1}}{(1+az^d)^2},
    \]
    so the two critical points are $0$ and $\infty$, each of multiplicity $d-1$, and $P_d(z)-z$ has a zero of order $3$ at $z=1$.

The accompanying notebook argument calls the welded fixed point both multiplicity $3$ and multiplicity $2$, so that cusp argument by itself is not a valid proof of rigidity. The needed centralizer statement follows directly: if an orientation-preserving circle homeomorphism $h$ commutes with $P_d$, it fixes the unique parabolic fixed point $1$. For every $n$, it preserves the finite cyclically ordered set $\operatorname{Fix}(P_d^{\circ n})$; an order-preserving permutation of this set that fixes $1$ is the identity. The repelling periodic points are dense in $J(P_d)=\mathbb S^1$, and hence $h=\operatorname{Id}$.

These three observations in conjunction establish some sense of rigidity as far as these objects' conjugacy classes are concerned. Now let us state the main theorem in which the core of McMullen's surgery resides.

To prove the Main Theorem we need to understand what kind of maps $f$ induces on the different components of the ideal boundary of $C$. We shall summarize that first in the following two propositions.

\subsection*{Proposition 6.16}{(Global Dynamics of $\hat{f}$ on $I(C)$)}:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item All but finitely many components of $\hat{\mathbb{C}}\backslash C$ map to their images by a conformal isomorphism.
        \item Every component of $I(C)$ is preperiodic and there are only finitely many periodic ones.
        \item For any component $I(U)$ of $I(C)$, there exist quasisymmetric maps $\hat{\phi}_1$ and $\hat{\phi}_2$ mapping $I(U)$ and $\hat{f}(I(U))$ respectively to $\mathbb{S}^1$ that provide an equivalence between $\hat{f}$ and $z\rightarrow z^d$ for some $d\geq 1$. If $I(U)$ is fixed, $\hat{f}$ and $z\rightarrow z^d$ may not be quasisymmetrically conjugate.
    \end{enumerate}
    (Note: The equivalence between $\hat{f}$  and $z\rightarrow z^d$ for some $d\geq 1$ can be changed to an equivalence between $\hat{f}$  and any Blaschke product of degree $d$ on $\mathbb{S}^1$. There is also a lot of freedom in the choices of the quasisymmetric maps $\hat{\phi}_1$ and $\hat{\phi}_2$ providing the equivalence, in that, for an arbitrary choice of one, one can obtain the other).

\subsection*{Proposition 6.17}{(Dynamics of $\hat{f}$ on Periodic Components of $I(C)$)}: On each periodic component of $I(C)$, the first return map is quasisymmetrically conjugate to one of the three rigid models.

Proof of Proposition $6.16$. There are only finitely many components $V_1, V_2,\ldots, V_k$ of $\hat{\mathbb{C}}\backslash C$ which intersect $f^{-1}(C)$ or contain a critical point. Set $\mathcal{V} = \{V_j\}_{1\leq j\leq k}$.\\
    Proof of (1). If $U$ is a component of $\hat{\mathbb{C}}\backslash C$ not in $\mathcal{V}$, then $f$ maps $U$ onto another component of $\hat{\mathbb{C}}\backslash C$ as a covering. Since $U$ is a disk, $f\big|_U$ is a conformal isomorphism onto its image. \\
    Proof of (2). Let $U$ be a component of $\hat{\mathbb{C}}\backslash C$ not in $\mathcal{V}$. Suppose $f^{\circ n}(U)$ is not in $\mathcal{V}$ for any $n\geq 0$. Then, $f^{\circ n}$ is normal on $U$ and therefore $f^{\circ n}(U)$ must eventually cycle, otherwise $U$ would be a wandering domain which \BlogPost{first-surgery}{Sullivan's No Wandering Theorem} rules out for a rational map. Hence, $U$ is eventually mapped onto a Fatou component whose first return map is a conformal isomorphism, and therefore a Siegel disk. It follows that $I(U)$ is preperiodic. If, on the other hand, $f^{\circ n}(U)$ is eventually mapped onto one of the components in $\mathcal{V}$ then $I(U)$ must also be preperiodic. Indeed, if some iterate is mapped onto $I(W)$ for $W \notin \mathcal{V}$, we can repeat the argument from before: the component $W$ is eventually mapped onto a Siegel disk or onto one of the components in $\mathcal{V}$. Since there are only finitely many components in $\mathcal{V}$, the ideal boundary $I(U)$ will eventually cycle. There is a finite number of periodic components in $I(C)$, since there are at most finitely many cycles of Siegel disks and finitely many components in $\mathcal{V}$ (as the number of cycles of indifferent points is finite).\\

But if $U=V$, then $z^d\not\sim\widehat f$, as the maps
    \[
    (\text{anything})\circ\phi_1\circ R_U
    \neq(\text{lift})\circ\phi_2\circ R_V.
    \]

When $U$ is fixed, independently choosing the two annular coordinates gives only a two-sided equivalence and need not give a conjugacy. This is precisely the periodic obstruction addressed by Proposition $6.17$.

Now let us devote some time to prove Proposition $6.17$ through a sequence of lemmas which shall study each type of periodic component of $I(C)$ separately. Let $U$ be a component of $\hat{\mathbb{C}}\backslash C$ for which $I(U)$ is periodic under $\hat{f}$. Replacing $f$ by a suitable iterate, we may assume that $I(U)$ is fixed. Recall from the discussion above that there is a collar annulus $U' \subset U$, whose boundary component facing $C$ represents $I(U)$, such that $f$ is a covering onto its image.
\subsection*{Lemma 6.18}: Suppose $\hat{f}(I(U)) = I(U)$. If $U'$ can be chosen to be a proper subset of $f(U')$ then $\hat{f}$ is quasisymmetrically conjugate to $z\rightarrow z^d$ for some $d>1$.

\textit{Proof.}: In the proof of the above lemma we shall use the following theorem. A complete treatment of the theorem and expanding maps can be found in \cite{shub1985expanding}, \cite{hubbard1982iteration} and \cite{de2012one}.
    \subsection*{Theorem 6.19}: Any expanding\footnote{A real-analytic endomorphism on $\mathbb{S}^1$ is said to be expanding if there is a smooth metric $\rho(\theta)\text{d}\theta$ with respect to which the derivative of the map is everywhere $>1$.} $C^{1+\alpha}$ orientation preserving endomorphism of $\mathbb{S}^1$ is quasisymmetrically conjugate to $z\rightarrow z^d$ for some $d>1$.

footnotes.source: A real-analytic endomorphism on $\mathbb{S}^1$ is said to be expanding if there is a smooth metric $\rho(\theta)\text{d}\theta$ with respect to which the derivative of the map is everywhere $>1$.

passages.source: Uniformize $U$. By the Schwarz Reflection Principle, the map in these coordinates extends to a holomorphic covering $F:A\rightarrow B$, where $A$ and $B$ are annuli containing $\mathbb{S}^1$ and $A$ is a proper subset of $B$. The covering is a local isometry between the Poincar\'e metrics of $A$ and $B$, while the Poincar\'e metric of $A$ is strictly larger than the one inherited from $B$. It follows that $F$ is expanding on $\mathbb{S}^1$ relative to the Poincar\'e metric of $B$. By Theorem $6.19$, the result follows.

For the symmetric annulus $\mathbb A_{R,1/R}=\{R<|z|<1/R\}$, $0<R<1$, the source calculation uses the Poincar\'e density
    \[
    \lambda_R(z)=\frac{\pi}{2\log(1/R)}
    \frac{1}{|z|\cos\!\left(\dfrac{\pi\log|z|}{2\log(1/R)}\right)}.
    \]
    The local-isometry identity is, with the domain and target densities distinguished,
    \[
    \lambda_B(F(z))|F'(z)|=\lambda_A(z).
    \]
    Since $A\subsetneq B$, monotonicity gives $\lambda_A>\lambda_B$ on $A$, which is the expansion used above on $\mathbb S^1$.

\subsection*{Lemma 6.20}: Suppose $\hat{f}: I(U) \rightarrow I(U)$. Either $\partial U \subset \partial V$ for some Fatou component $V \subset U$ or $\hat{f}:I(U)\rightarrow I(U)$ is quasisymmetrically conjugate to $z\rightarrow z^d$ for some $d>1$.

\textit{Proof.}: To prove this lemma we shall need the following theorem due to Zoretti which can be found in \cite{whyburn1948analytic}.
    \subsection*{Theorem 6.21}{(Zoretti's Theorem)}: Let $C$ be a component of a compact set $J \subset \mathbb{R}^2$. For all $\epsilon >0$ there exists a simple closed curve $\gamma_{\epsilon}$ which encloses $C$ and is such that $\gamma_{\epsilon}\cap J = \emptyset$ and $\text{dist}(C, x) < \epsilon$ for all $x\in \gamma_{\epsilon}$.

Suppose first that $\partial U$ is not contained in the boundary of any Fatou component in $U$. In $\overline{U}$, $\partial U$ is a component of $\overline{U}\cap\overline{J(f)}$ $\implies$ one can apply Zoretti's Theorem to get simple closed curves $\gamma_n$ in the Fatou set, each lying in an $\epsilon_n$-neighbourhood of $\partial U$, where $\epsilon_n\rightarrow 0$. These curves lie in infinitely many distinct Fatou components. Since there are only finitely many periodic Fatou components, choose $n$ large enough that $\gamma_n$ lies in an aperiodic component and the annulus $V'$ bounded by $\gamma_n$ and $\partial U$ contains no critical values.\\
    There is a unique component $U'$ of $f^{-1}(V')$ in $U$, bounded by $\partial U$ and a preimage of $\gamma_n$. Since $\gamma_n$ lies in an aperiodic component, it is disjoint from its preimage $\implies$ either $U'\subset V'$ or $V'\subset U'$; equality cannot hold. But $f:U'\rightarrow V'$ is a proper covering and $\text{mod}(U')\leq\text{mod}(V')$. This gives us that $U'$ is a proper subset of $V' = f(U')$, and the lemma follows from the previous lemma.

Now we are left to handle the cases $\partial U \subset \partial V$, where $V \subset U$ is a Fatou component. By the classification theorem of periodic Fatou components for rational maps, $V$ can only be a Siegel disk, a Herman ring, a basin of (super)attraction, or a parabolic basin. We deal with these cases separately in a bunch of lemmas to follow.

\subsection*{Lemma 6.22}: If $V$ is fixed Siegel disk or a fixed Herman ring of rotation number $\theta \in \mathbb{R}\backslash\mathbb{Q}$, then $\hat{f}$ is real analytically conjugate to the rigid rotation $R_{\theta} = e^{2\pi i \theta}z$

\textit{Proof.}: If $V$ is a Siegel disk then $U=V$ and a Riemann mapping $R_U$, which maps the indifferent fixed point to $0$, conjugates $f$ to the rigid rotation on $\mathbb{D}$. Hence $\hat{f}$ on $\mathbb{S}^1$ is actually equal to $R_{\theta}$. If $V$ is a Herman ring, then there is a conformal map $\phi:V \rightarrow \mathbb{A}_r$ conjugating $f$ to $R_{\theta}$. In this case, arguing as we did in Proposition $6.16$, we obtain that $\hat{f}$ on $I(U)$ is real analytically conjugate to $R_{\theta}$.

\subsection*{Lemma 6.23}: If $V$ is an immediate basin of (super)attraction, or a parabolic basin whose parabolic fixed point is not on $\partial U$, then $\hat{f}$ is quasisymmetrically conjugate to $z\rightarrow z^d$ for some $d>1$.

\textit{Proof.}: Let $W \subset V$ be a Jordan domain, for which $f(W)$ is a proper subset of $W$ and $\overline{W}$ does not intersect $\partial U$. In the (super)attraction case $W$ may be chosen as disk surrounding the (super)attracting fixed point and mapping inside itself. In the parabolic case $W$ may be chosen as an attracting petal in the parabolic basin so that $\overline{W}$ intersects $\partial V$ at the parabolic fixed point.\\
    Let $W_n$ be the component of $f^{\circ (-n)}(W)$ containing $W$, then
    $$\overline{W} \subset \overline{W_1} \subset \overline{W_2} \subset \ldots
    $$

and $\bigcup_{n}{W_n} = V$. In the parabolic case, $\partial U$ cannot contain any point in the grand orbit of the parabolic point since $f(\partial U) = \partial U$, so $W_n \cap \partial U = \emptyset$ for all $n>0$. Observe that, if $V$ is not simply connected, $W_n$ will become multiply connected after a certain $n_0$, since the union of all the $W_n$'s must account for all of $V$.\\
    For every $n$, there is a component of $\partial W_n$ which together with $\partial U$ bounds an annulus $A_n$ disjoint from $W_n$. In general, $A_n$ may contain infinitely many different components of the Julia set. Each annulus lies in an $\epsilon_n$-neighbourhood of $\partial U$, where $\epsilon_n \rightarrow 0$ as $n\rightarrow \infty$. Otherwise there is a continuum in $\partial V$ which lies in $U$ and meets $\partial U$, contradicting the fact that $C$ is a component of the Julia set.\\
    Choose $n$ sufficiently large so that $A_n$ contains no critical values. The component of $\partial W_n$ which, together with $\partial U$, bounds $A_n$ is essentially the component that hits rays from $\partial U$ to $W_n$ first. This fact, along with $f(W_{n+1}) = W_n$, ensures that $A_{n+1}$ is a component of $f^{-1}(A_n)$ and a proper subset of $A_n$. Lemma $6.18$ now applies.
\subsection*{Lemma 6.24}: If $V$ belongs to a parabolic basin, with a parabolic fixed point on $\partial U$, then $\hat{f}$ on $I(U)$ is quasisymmetrically conjugate to $P_d(z)$ for some $d>1$.

\textit{Proof.}: Let $R_U:U\rightarrow \mathbb{D}$ be a Riemann map, normalized so that the parabolic fixed prime end corresponds to $z=1$. Then the coordinate form of $f$, together with $V$, carries over to $\mathbb{D}$, where we continue to denote them by $f$ and $V$. Observe that this coordinate form of $f$ is defined only on a subset of the disk, and that its domain contains $V$ and a one-sided neighbourhood of $\mathbb{S}^1$. By the Schwarz Reflection Principle, it can be extended to a holomorphic map on a neighbourhood of $\mathbb{S}^1$ having a parabolic fixed point at $z=1$. The restriction to the unit circle is precisely $\hat{f}$. We construct by hand a quasisymmetric conjugacy between $\hat{f}$ and $P_d$, where $d$ is the degree of $\hat{f}$ on $\mathbb{S}^1$.\\

The final notebook page proposes the following rigour step: first extend $\Psi_n$ smoothly to the rest of the annulus bounded by $\mathbb S^1$ and $\gamma_n$, obtaining $\widehat\Psi_n$, and then claim $\widehat\Psi_n\to\Psi$ because $H^1(\widetilde U)$ is Cauchy complete. Completeness alone does not show that $\langle\widehat\Psi_n\rangle$ is Cauchy, and the notes supply no uniform quasiconformal or $H^1$ estimate. Thus the recursive parabolic construction above faithfully records the source, but its limiting-extension step remains a localized gap unless that standard uniform estimate is supplied.
Let us apply Propositions $6.16$ and $6.17$ in a sequence of surgeries to establish the main theorem.

Proof of Main Theorem. Suppose $I(U)$ is periodic of period $p\geq 1$. Following Proposition $6.17$, let $\hat{\phi}:I(U)\rightarrow \mathbb{S}^1$ be a quasisymmetric map so that $\hat{\phi}\circ \hat{f}^p\circ \hat{\phi}^{-1}$ equals exactly one of the rigid models, say $B_U$. Choose a Riemann mapping $R_U:U \rightarrow \mathbb{D}$. The ideal boundary values of $R_U$ identify $I(U)$ with $\mathbb{S}^1$, so $\hat{\phi}$ determines a quasisymmetric self-map of the circle. Extend this self-map quasiconformally over $\mathbb{D}$ and compose it with $R_U$ to obtain $\phi:U\rightarrow\mathbb{D}$. It follows that $f^{\circ p}$ and $B_U$ are compatible on the ideal boundary via $\phi$. If $p=1$ this periodic component is dealt with: replacing $f$ on $U$ by the map $\phi^{-1}\circ B_U\circ \phi$ and keeping $f$ outside $U$, it follows from the \BlogPost{third-surgery}{Gluing Lemma} that we obtain a new quasirational map. If $p>1$ then we have to replace $f$ on the disc components $U_j$ where $I(U_j):= \hat{f}^j(I(U))$ for $0\leq j\leq p-1$ with maps that are compatible with $\hat{f}$ along the ideal boundaries and whose composition agrees with $\phi^{-1}\circ B_U\circ \phi$ on $U$. Set $U_0=U$ and $U_p=U_0$. Let $d_j\geq 1$ denote the degree of $\hat{f}:I(U_j)\rightarrow I(U_{j+1})$ for $0\leq j\leq p-1$. Then the product $\prod_{j=0}^{p-1}{d_j} = d$, where $d=1$ in the elliptic case. From Proposition $6.16$ $(3)$ we know that there exists a pair of quasisymmetric maps mapping $I(U_j)$ and $I(U_{j+1})$ respectively to $\mathbb{S}^1$ and providing an equivalence between $\hat{f}$ and $B_j(z):= z^{d_j}$ for $0\leq j\leq p-2$. From what we noted in Proposition $6.16$ we know that we may choose one of the quasisymmetric maps arbitrarily. Let $\hat{\phi}_0 = \hat{\phi}:I(U_0)\rightarrow \mathbb{S}^1$ from above and let $\phi_0=\phi$. For $j = 1,\ldots, p-1$ establish recursively $\hat{\phi}_j:I(U_j)\rightarrow \mathbb{S}^1$ such that $\hat{\phi}_j\circ \hat{f} = B_{j-1}\circ \hat{\phi}_{j-1}$. Extend $\hat{\phi}_1,\ldots,\hat{\phi}_{p-1}$ quasiconformally over their disks and denote the extensions by $\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_{p-1}$. Finally set $\phi_p=\phi_0$. Depending on the case we choose $B_{p-1}$ to be the Blaschke product defined as

$$B_{p-1}(z):= \begin{cases}
        e^{2\pi i \theta}z, &\quad\text{in the elliptic case,}\\
        z^{d_{p-1}} &\quad\text{in the hyperbolic case,}\\
        \frac{z^{d_{p-1}}+a}{1 + az^{d_{p-1}}} &\quad\text{in the parabolic case, for}   a = \frac{d-1}{d+1}\\
        \end{cases}$$

        e^{2\pi i \theta}z, &\quad\text{in the elliptic case,}\\

        \frac{z^{d_{p-1}}+a}{1 + az^{d_{p-1}}} &\quad\text{in the parabolic case, for}   a = \frac{d-1}{d+1}\\

With $B_j(z)=z^{d_j}$ for $0\leq j\leq p-2$, the corrected telescoping identity behind the source's factor table is
    \[
    g^{\circ p}\big|_{U_0}
      =\phi_0^{-1}\circ
        \bigl(B_{p-1}\circ B_{p-2}\circ\cdots\circ B_0\bigr)
        \circ\phi_0,
    \qquad d=\prod_{j=0}^{p-1}d_j.
    \]
    The model factors are displayed together as
    \[
    \begin{array}{c|ccccc}
    B_U&B_{p-1}&B_{p-2}&B_{p-3}&\cdots&B_0\\ \hline
    e^{2\pi i\theta}z&e^{2\pi i\theta}z&z&z&\cdots&z\\
    z^d&z^{d_{p-1}}&z^{d_{p-2}}&z^{d_{p-3}}&\cdots&z^{d_0}\\
    P_d&M_a\circ(z\mapsto z^{d_{p-1}})&z^{d_{p-2}}&z^{d_{p-3}}&\cdots&z^{d_0}
    \end{array}
    \]
    where $M_a(z)=(z+a)/(1+az)$ and $a=(d-1)/(d+1)$. This corrects the source's use of a sum of degrees and its mismatched $B_p$ indices.

The conditions in \BlogPost{third-surgery}{Corollary $6.13$} are therefore satisfied. Hence, by replacing $f$ on $U_j$ by the map $\phi_{j+1}^{-1}\circ B_j\circ \phi_j$ for $j = 0, 1, \ldots, p-1$ and keeping $f$ outside $\bigcup_{j=0}^{p-1}{U_j}$ we obtain a new quasirational map.\\
    After having dealt with all the periodic components of $I(C)$ we work backwards along the preimages of each of them. If $I(V)$ is one of them, and $\hat{f}(I(V)) = I(W)$, then $\hat{f}$ is quasisymmetrically equivalent to $z\rightarrow z^d$ for some $d\geq 1$. If $d=1$ we keep the conformal isomorphism $f\big|_V:V\rightarrow W$. Only if $d>1$ shall we replace the map. Suppose this has been done up to $V$. We construct as before gluing maps $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$ using Riemann mappings $R_V$ and $R_W$, and define the new map on $V$ by $\phi_2^{-1}\circ z^d\circ \phi_1$. The new critical point $c$ equals $\phi_1^{-1}(0) \in V$, with critical value equal to $\phi_2^{-1}(0)$. The orbit of $c$ satisfies one of the conditions in the main theorem if the orbit of its critical value does. We choose the Riemann mapping $R_W$ so that $\phi_2^{-1}(0)$ has the correct orbital behaviour. Keep repeating this. By Proposition $6.16$ (1), after a finite number of steps we have constructed a quasirational map $q$ satisfying the conditions of the main theorem. After integration, let $\Phi$ be a quasiconformal map such that $\Phi\circ q=g\circ\Phi$ for the desired rational map $g$.\\

The preceding lemmas prove Proposition $6.17$, and the surgery construction proves Theorem $6.15$. Therefore, the stable conjugacy establishes the isomorphism $\text{Mod}(C, f) \cong \text{Mod}(J(g), g)$ and proves Theorem $6.3$ (1). The following proposition shall handle Theorem $6.3$ (2), thereby finishing the proof of the central theorem behind this surgery.
